title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models
one_liner: By carefully removing pieces of a time-series model, you discover that many layers do nothing and certain attention heads copy old patterns instead of learning new ones.
lead: When a trained time-series model reads a sequence of numbers (like daily temperature or stock prices), it passes the data through many layers. The question the paper answers is: do all these layers actually matter, or do some do redundant work? By testing what happens when you turn off entire layers and specific focus units (called attention heads, which are small pieces that learn to pay attention to certain time steps), the authors uncover which parts of the model are truly working and which ones just copy old patterns from memory.

problem.h2: Models get big and bloated without anyone asking why
paras: Time series foundation models are trained on millions of examples to predict things like temperature tomorrow or stock price next week. These models have many layers—sometimes dozens—that transform the numbers step by step. The naive assumption is that each layer does essential work.

But what if many layers are just wasting compute? And what if some layers are actually hurting by copying old patterns instead of learning something new? A beginner might guess that you can just remove a layer and the model breaks. In reality, the model often keeps working almost as well. That tells you the layer was redundant.

The real problem: you have no clear way to find which exact parts of the model are redundant, and which parts cause specific bad behaviors like copying motifs (repeating the same pattern) or always predicting seasonality even when it is wrong.

callout.html: Systematically turn off layers and attention heads (the mechanisms that focus on specific time steps) and measure whether the model still works; use a math framework to predict which heads will be redundant.

steps.text: Remove layer by layer; measure how prediction accuracy changes.
Attention heads are sub-units that each focus on certain time steps; turn each off and measure.
For each head, compute a math score that predicts how replaceable it is.
Heads with very low stable rank are the ones that do redundant work or copy patterns.
Remove those heads and confirm the model still works (or works better), because low-rank heads contribute nothing or only hurt.

paras: The paper modifies which layers and focus units stay in the model. A focus unit is a small computation unit (called an attention head) that learns to look at certain time steps when making a prediction. By removing redundant layers and focus units, the authors create a leaner model.

hidden.name: Stable rank
paras: For each attention head, you can write down the mathematical matrix (a grid of numbers) that describes what that head does. The stable rank is a single number that measures how 'full' or 'effective' that matrix is. A high stable rank means the head is doing unique, non-redundant work. A low stable rank means the head is mostly redundant—its output is determined by just a few key patterns, or it is just repeating old data.

The paper estimates stable rank directly from the learned weights (the numbers the model learned during training) using a kernel regressor framework—a way to understand these models as systems that fit curves through the data. Heads with stable rank close to 1 are the problematic ones: they copy old patterns instead of reasoning about new time series.

heat.caption: Darker means higher stable rank, irreplaceable work. Lightest means close to 1, copying or redundant.

reads.html: Stable rank tells you whether an attention head is doing real work or just repeating patterns from memory.
The authors frame these models as kernel regressors and compute stable rank via the per-head projection matrices to identify degenerate heads.

mechanism.h2: Why removing redundant parts keeps the model working
paras: When a model has redundant layers, one layer can often do the job of two. Imagine layer 5 learns to recognize a pattern, then layer 6 also learns the same pattern. Layer 6 is wasting compute. If you remove layer 6, layer 5 is still there doing the work, so the output barely changes.

Attention heads that copy old patterns (like always predicting yesterday's temperature) are even more harmful: they hurt accuracy because they ignore what is actually happening now. These low-rank heads have very little flexibility—they are locked into one behavior. By removing them, the model is forced to learn something more adaptive. The stable rank number predicts which heads are this rigid and redundant.

stages.s: Layer 2 learns the same feature again
Remove Layer 2; output still the same

math.words: Stable rank equals the sum of all eigenvalues squared, divided by the largest eigenvalue squared. A matrix is redundant if stable rank is close to 1.
symbols: A number from 1 to the number of columns, measuring how much work the head does.
The hidden patterns inside the projection matrix, sorted by strength.
The strongest pattern the head learned.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an attention head's projection matrix has singular values [10, 8, 2, 1].
Sum of all values: 10 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 21. Sum squared: 21^2 = 441.
This head uses most of its potential—it is doing real work, not redundant.
Now suppose a head has singular values [10, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1] (very imbalanced).
Sum = 10.9. Sum squared = 118.81. Largest = 10. Largest squared = 100.
This head is locked into one behavior—it is copying, not reasoning.

math.note: Heads with stable rank near 1 are the ones freezing into a single repeated pattern, like always predicting seasonality; removing them forces the model to learn adaptive behavior.

charts.title: Before removing redundant heads
charts.note: The model seems to work overall but certain heads cause systematic errors.

charts.title: After removing low stable-rank heads
charts.note: Slightly lower overall accuracy (one point), but the systematic biases vanish because the copying heads are gone.

items.html: If you remove all low-rank heads at once, you might lose real predictive power for specific tasks. The model adapts, but accuracy drops.
The cutoff for 'redundant' (e.g., stable rank less than 2) varies across architectures and datasets. What is redundant in one model is essential in another.
If a time series truly does repeat (like daily temperature patterns), a head that learns seasonality is helpful, not harmful. The method finds it anyway.

Compute stable rank for each head; remove only the absolute lowest (because those are the most expendable); measure accuracy before and after; keep the heads that preserve or improve performance, because some low-rank heads turn out to be helpful for certain datasets.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a time series foundation model (like one trained to predict electricity demand or traffic speed). Compute the stable rank of every attention head. Sort heads by stable rank from lowest to highest. Starting with the very lowest, remove one head at a time and re-evaluate the model on a held-out test dataset. Plot how test accuracy changes. You should see: the very lowest-rank heads can be removed with zero accuracy loss (or small loss), and removing them often eliminates the copying behavior (e.g., prediction errors caused by blindly repeating seasonality).
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_loss = accuracy_before - accuracy_after (after removing head H); copying_error = fraction of predictions that repeat motifs from context exactly
demo.closing: The demo makes it impossible to miss that the lowest stable-rank heads are redundant (because removing them has zero or positive effect on accuracy) and that removing them reduces degenerate behaviors (because those heads were locked into copying patterns, not adapting).
